title: Visuals in persuasive texts

match.reason: The bank point classifies texts by purpose (imaginative, persuasive, informative), while the new point teaches how visuals such as cartoons, photos and graphics persuade, so it is a different idea.

draft.title: Visuals in persuasive texts
card: Writers often pair words with a visual, such as a cartoon, a photo or a graphic. The visual is chosen to push readers toward the writer's view.
uses exaggeration and humour to mock a person or an idea. A cartoon might draw a council leader as a tiny figure behind a huge desk to make them look out of touch.
can shock or move readers by showing a real scene, such as a dry, cracked riverbed. Its angle, framing and what it leaves out all shape the response.
such as a chart or infographic, shows facts in a clear form. It can make a trend look urgent and supports the claims in the written text.
draft.remember: A visual is chosen to persuade: it can mock, shock or back up the words.

a.q: A newspaper cartoon draws a mayor as a giant with a tiny head, stamping on small shops. What is the cartoon mainly doing?
opts: Supporting the mayor with a chart of facts
Showing a real scene to shock readers
Presenting the issue in a neutral way
a.why: Drawing the mayor as a distorted giant exaggerates features to make the mayor look foolish and harmful. This is mockery. It is not a photo of a real scene, and it is not neutral because it takes a side.
a.clue: Think about what exaggeration in a drawing does to its subject.

b.q: An opinion piece argues that a town needs more bus services. Beside it is a photo of an elderly man waiting alone at a bus stop in heavy rain. What is the most likely purpose of the photo?
opts: To stir sympathy and back up the written argument
To prove the argument with a full set of statistics
To mock the people who disagree with the writer
To give a balanced view of both sides of the issue
b.why: The photo shows a vulnerable person in a hard situation, so it stirs sympathy and backs up the words. A single photo is not a full set of statistics, and nothing in it mocks opponents. The writer chose it to support one side.
b.clue: Ask what feeling the photo creates and which side it helps.

b.best: To stir sympathy and back up the written argument
